prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- Lebanon's prime minister condemned the firing of rockets into northern Israel after an attack wounded two Israelis on Thursday.  He said his government is trying to determine who was responsible. U.N. soldiers on Thursday inspect the site in Lebanon thought to be the source of rockets fired into Israel. Israel's military warned Israeli civilians to stick close to shelters after police said at least four rockets hit near the city of Nahariya, about 6 miles (10 kilometers) south of the Lebanese border. The Israeli military said it returned fire across the border with mortars. Schools and kindergartens were closed in Nahariya and the nearby town of Shlomi, the Israel Defense Forces reported. "What happened in the south [of Lebanon] is a violation of Resolution 1701 and is rejected by Lebanon," Lebanese Prime Minister Fouad Siniora said, referring to the U.N. resolution that ended the 2006 conflict between Israel and Lebanon's Hezbollah militia. In a statement issued by his office, Siniora said he has asked Lebanese authorities to investigate the attack alongside troops from the U.N. peacekeeping force deployed along the border. He also condemned the Israeli retaliatory strikes, which the Lebanese military said inflicted no casualties.  Watch CNN's Christiane Amanpour discuss rocket attack » . There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attacks, which came as Israeli airstrikes on Gaza, to the south, entered a 13th day. The Israeli campaign in Gaza is aimed at halting rocket fire from the Hamas-ruled Palestinian territory. Israel fought a similar battle against the Lebanese Shiite Muslim militia Hezbollah in 2006, during which Hezbollah rained rockets on cities in Israeli's north for a month before a cease-fire was reached. But Hezbollah has kept a tight rein on its forces in southern Lebanon since the cease-fire, and a number of Palestinian factions operate in southern Lebanon as well. Andrea Tenenti, a spokesman for UNIFIL, the U.N. peacekeeping mission in Lebanon, said the rockets appear to have been fired from a point about 4.5 miles east of Naqoura, where the peacekeepers are headquartered. "We've been intensifying our patrols on the ground in order to prevent any further incident," Tenenti said. He said UNIFIL's commander, Maj. Gen. Claudio Graziano, is in "constant and close contact" with both sides "and has urged maximum restraint in order to prevent any escalation of the situation." CNN's Michal Zippori in Jerusalem and Cal Perry and Nada Husseini in Beirut contributed to this report.

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) — Lebanon’s prime minister denounced the launch of rockets into northern Israel after two Israelis were injured in an attack on Thursday, saying his government was working to identify those behind it.

On Thursday, U.N. troops examined an area in Lebanon believed to have been the launch site for rockets fired into Israel.

Israel’s military advised civilians in northern Israel to remain near shelters after police reported that at least four rockets landed near Nahariya, a city about 6 miles (10 kilometers) south of the Lebanese border. The Israeli military said it responded by firing mortar rounds across the frontier.

According to the Israel Defense Forces, schools and kindergartens were shut in Nahariya and in the nearby town of Shlomi.

Lebanese Prime Minister Fouad Siniora said the incident in southern Lebanon violated U.N. Resolution 1701 and was unacceptable to Lebanon. The resolution brought an end to the 2006 war between Israel and Lebanon’s Hezbollah militia.

In a statement released by his office, Siniora said he had instructed Lebanese authorities to look into the rocket fire in coordination with soldiers from the U.N. peacekeeping force stationed along the border. He also criticized Israel’s retaliatory fire, which Lebanon’s military said caused no casualties.

Watch CNN’s Christiane Amanpour discuss the rocket attack »

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the launches. They occurred as Israeli airstrikes in Gaza, to the south, continued into their 13th day. Israel says its operation in Gaza is intended to stop rocket attacks from the Hamas-controlled Palestinian territory.

In 2006, Israel fought a comparable conflict against Hezbollah, the Lebanese Shiite Muslim militia. During that war, Hezbollah fired rockets at cities across northern Israel for a month before a cease-fire was reached.

Since that cease-fire, however, Hezbollah has maintained strict control over its fighters in southern Lebanon. Several Palestinian factions also operate in the area.

Andrea Tenenti, a spokesman for UNIFIL, the U.N. peacekeeping operation in Lebanon, said the rockets seemed to have been launched from a location roughly 4.5 miles east of Naqoura, where the peacekeeping force has its headquarters.

“We’ve been intensifying our patrols on the ground in order to prevent any further incident,” Tenenti said.

He added that UNIFIL commander Maj. Gen. Claudio Graziano remained in “constant and close contact” with both sides and had called for “maximum restraint” to avoid any worsening of the situation.

CNN’s Michal Zippori in Jerusalem, along with Cal Perry and Nada Husseini in Beirut, contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.output:
**BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN)** — Rockets fired from southern Lebanon struck northern Israel on Thursday, prompting Israeli forces to respond with artillery fire and raising fears that the conflict in Gaza could spill across another volatile border.

Lebanese Prime Minister Fouad Siniora condemned the rocket attack, saying Lebanon rejected any attempt to use its territory as a launchpad for attacks that could drag the country into a wider confrontation. His government moved quickly to distance itself from the fire, which came amid heightened regional anger over Israel’s military offensive in the Gaza Strip.

The Israeli military said several rockets landed in the Galilee region of northern Israel. There were no immediate reports of serious casualties, though residents in the area were told to take shelter as sirens sounded. Israel responded by firing artillery shells toward the suspected launch area in southern Lebanon.

The United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL, said it was working with both the Lebanese Armed Forces and the Israeli military to determine who fired the rockets and to prevent further escalation. UN peacekeepers increased patrols in the area, while Lebanese troops searched for additional launch sites.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the rocket fire. Hezbollah, the powerful Lebanese militant and political movement that fought a monthlong war with Israel in 2006, did not claim involvement. The incident nevertheless underscored the fragility of the border region, where any exchange of fire carries the risk of reigniting a broader conflict.

The rocket attack came as Israel continued its offensive against Hamas in Gaza, an operation that has sparked protests across the Arab world and intensified pressure on governments allied with the West. In Lebanon, where memories of the 2006 war remain raw, officials have sought to avoid being pulled into a new confrontation with Israel.

Siniora’s condemnation reflected that concern. Lebanese officials said the country remained committed to U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, which ended the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war and calls for southern Lebanon to remain free of unauthorized armed groups.

UNIFIL urged restraint on all sides, warning that even isolated rocket fire could destabilize the already tense border.

The exchange marked one of the most serious cross-border incidents since the 2006 war, though both Israel and Lebanon appeared to signal that they did not want the confrontation to widen.

### Rockets Fired From Lebanon Into Israel Amid Gaza Offensive

Rockets were fired from southern Lebanon into northern Israel during Israel’s military offensive in Gaza, raising concerns that the conflict could widen beyond the Palestinian territory.

Israeli officials said rockets launched from Lebanon landed in northern Israel, prompting Israeli forces to respond with artillery fire toward the launch area. There were no immediate reports of major casualties, though the incident heightened tensions along one of the region’s most sensitive borders.

The United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, known as UNIFIL, monitored the situation along the frontier. UNIFIL spokesman Andrea Tenenti said the peacekeeping mission was in contact with both the Lebanese and Israeli sides and was working to determine the circumstances of the rocket fire. UNIFIL typically urges restraint after such incidents and works with the parties to prevent escalation along the Blue Line, the U.N.-demarcated boundary between Lebanon and Israel.

There was no immediate indication that Hezbollah, the powerful Lebanese Shiite militant and political organization, had claimed responsibility. In previous flare-ups, smaller Palestinian factions operating in Lebanon have sometimes been blamed for sporadic rocket attacks into Israel.

The incident came as Israel was engaged in a major offensive in Gaza against Hamas and other militant groups. Periods of intense fighting in Gaza have often triggered solidarity protests and occasional cross-border fire elsewhere in the region, including from Lebanon.

### Background: The 2006 Israel-Hezbollah War

The Israel-Lebanon border remains highly volatile because of the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah. That conflict began after Hezbollah fighters crossed into Israel, killed several Israeli soldiers and captured two others. Israel responded with a large-scale military campaign in Lebanon, while Hezbollah fired thousands of rockets into northern Israel.

The 34-day war killed more than 1,000 people in Lebanon, most of them civilians, and more than 150 Israelis, including soldiers and civilians. It ended with U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, which called for a cessation of hostilities, the deployment of the Lebanese army in southern Lebanon, and an expanded UNIFIL presence.

Since then, the border has remained mostly quieter than during the war, but periodic rocket launches, Israeli responses, and Hezbollah-Israel tensions have kept the risk of renewed conflict alive.
